Bayesian Area-Level Small Area Estimation with INLA

Source: vignettes/hb-area-inla.Rmd
hb-area-inla.Rmd

Introduction

Classical Small Area Estimation (SAE) models—such as the Fay-Herriot (1979) model—traditionally assume a Gaussian distribution for direct survey estimators with known sampling error variances. However, real-world official statistics frequently encounter non-Gaussian indicators: - Poverty rates, unemployment rates, and prevalence ratios: strictly bounded in the open interval (0,1)(0, 1). - Disease counts, crime incidents, and rare events: discrete counts subject to Poisson or Negative Binomial overdispersion with population exposures. - Binary survey aggregates: proportions derived from small sample sizes (Binomial trials). - Skewed economic expenditures: strictly positive continuous outcomes (Gamma).

Furthermore, when data are collected across geographical areas and repeated over time (panel/longitudinal surveys), outcomes exhibit both spatial dependency and temporal autocorrelation.

The fastsae package introduces hb_area(), a unified hierarchical Bayesian framework powered by Integrated Nested Laplace Approximations (INLA). It provides fast deterministic approximations of the posterior marginals, without the chains, warm-up and tuning of Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC); against long Stan runs with the same model and priors its posterior means and SDs agreed closely (see the Engines section of ?hb_area).

Supported Distribution Families

hb_area() supports 6 probability distributions for the direct response:

Family Typical SAE Use Case Required Sampling Input Model Scale Parameter
"gaussian" Continuous indicators (e.g., mean income, mean years of schooling) vardir (sampling variance DdD_d) Inverted sampling variance scale=1/Dd\text{scale} = 1/D_d
"beta" Rates and proportions strictly in (0,1)(0, 1) vardir or trials Precision ϕd=μ̂d(1−μ̂d)/Vd−1\phi_d = \hat\mu_d(1 - \hat\mu_d)/V_d - 1 from a first fit (Janicki, 2020), or nd−1n_d - 1 from trials
"poisson" Counts and rare event rates exposure (expected count / population offset) Log-link offset log⁡(Ed)\log(E_d)
"nbinomial" Overdispersed counts and clustered events exposure; optional vardir Log-link offset; size μ̂d2/(Vd−μ̂d)\hat\mu_d^2/(V_d - \hat\mu_d) from a first fit when vardir is given
"binomial" Aggregated binary proportions trials (domain sample size ndn_d) Number of trials per domain
"gamma" Positive, right-skewed indicators (e.g., expenditures) vardir Precision (shape) yd2/Vdy_d^2/V_d

Mathematical Formulation

The hierarchical Bayesian model underlying hb_area() extends the classical Fay-Herriot framework to handle non-Gaussian responses and structured random effects. The model comprises three levels:

Level 1: Sampling Model (Likelihood)

For domain dd with direct estimator ydy_d and known sampling variance DdD_d:

π(yd∣ηd)=ExpFamily(yd∣ηd,Dd)\pi(y_d \mid \eta_d) = \text{ExpFamily}(y_d \mid \eta_d, D_d)

The link function connects the linear predictor ηd\eta_d to the mean μd=E(yd)\mu_d = E(y_d):

Family Link Function Linear Predictor
Gaussian Identity: ηd=μd\eta_d = \mu_d ηd=xd⊤β+ud\eta_d = x_d^\top \beta + u_d
Beta Logit: ηd=log⁡(μd/(1−μd))\eta_d = \log(\mu_d / (1-\mu_d)) ηd=xd⊤β+ud\eta_d = x_d^\top \beta + u_d
Poisson Log: ηd=log⁡(μd)\eta_d = \log(\mu_d) ηd=xd⊤β+ud+log⁡(Ed)\eta_d = x_d^\top \beta + u_d + \log(E_d)
Binomial Logit: ηd=log⁡(μd/(1−μd))\eta_d = \log(\mu_d / (1-\mu_d)) ηd=xd⊤β+ud\eta_d = x_d^\top \beta + u_d
Negative Binomial Log: ηd=log⁡(μd)\eta_d = \log(\mu_d) ηd=xd⊤β+ud+log⁡(Ed)\eta_d = x_d^\top \beta + u_d + \log(E_d)
Gamma Log: ηd=log⁡(μd)\eta_d = \log(\mu_d) ηd=xd⊤β+ud\eta_d = x_d^\top \beta + u_d

Level 2: Prior on Fixed Effects

β0∝1,βj∼N(0,1000),j=1,…,p\beta_0 \propto 1, \qquad \beta_j \sim N(0, 1000), \quad j = 1, \ldots, p

The intercept has INLA’s flat prior and the other coefficients a normal prior with variance 1000, which is nearly flat on the scale of most covariates.

Level 3: Prior on Random Effects

u∣σu∼N(0,σu2R−),σu∼half-normal(s)u \mid \sigma_u \sim N(0, \sigma_u^2 R^{-}), \qquad \sigma_u \sim \text{half-normal}(s)

The random effects u=(u1,…,um)⊤u = (u_1, \ldots, u_m)^\top follow a zero-mean Gaussian Markov random field whose structure matrix RR encodes the chosen spatial or temporal dependence (R=IR = I for iid effects; Besag, BYM2, RW1 and so on otherwise). The scale of the half-normal prior on their standard deviation is s=sd(y)s = \mathrm{sd}(y), the standard deviation of the direct estimates, for Gaussian models and s=1s = 1 on the logit or log scale for the other families. The further hyperparameters (the BYM2 mixing parameter, autocorrelations, dispersion parameters) and the reasons for these defaults are listed in vignette("hb-priors"); inla_engine() replaces any of them.

INLA Approximation

Rather than MCMC sampling, INLA approximates the posterior marginals of the hyperparameters θ\theta and of the latent field x=(β,u)x = (\beta, u) (Rue et al., 2009):

π̃(θ∣y)∝π(x,θ,y)π̃G(x∣θ,y)|x=x*(θ)\tilde{\pi}(\theta \mid y) \propto \left. \frac{\pi(x, \theta, y)}{\tilde{\pi}_G(x \mid \theta, y)} \right|_{x = x^*(\theta)}

where π̃G\tilde{\pi}_G is the Gaussian approximation of the full conditional of xx and x*(θ)x^*(\theta) its mode, and

π̃(xd∣y)=∑kπ̃(xd∣θk,y)π̃(θk∣y)Δk\tilde{\pi}(x_d \mid y) = \sum_k \tilde{\pi}(x_d \mid \theta_k, y) \, \tilde{\pi}(\theta_k \mid y) \, \Delta_k

where the integrals are evaluated using Laplace approximations and numerical integration. Three computational strategies are available through hb_area(..., engine = inla_engine(strategy = ...)), which also takes the priors and any further INLA::inla() arguments:

  • strategy = "gaussian": Fastest, best for well-behaved problems
  • strategy = "laplace": Default, good accuracy/speed balance
  • strategy = "simplified.laplace": Slightly faster Laplace, good for large models

The same models can be fitted by MCMC on CPU or GPU with engine = jax_engine() (NumPyro NUTS on JAX; see ?jax_engine). An MCMC fit is only usable when its chains have converged. The fit reports the rank-normalized R-hat and the effective sample size (ESS) of every parameter (Vehtari et al., 2021) and warns when R-hat is at least 1.05, the ESS is below 100 per chain, or there are divergent transitions; the trace and rank plots show which parameter is the problem:

fit_jax <- hb_area(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3,
  data = mys, vardir = "vardir",
  engine = jax_engine(chains = 4, samples = 1000)
)
fit_jax$rhat_max # below 1.01 is recommended
fit_jax$ess_min # above 100 per chain
head(fit_jax$mcmc_diagnostics) # R-hat and ESS of each parameter
autoplot(fit_jax, type = "rank") # chains near the dashed line: mixed
autoplot(fit_jax, type = "trace", pars = c("sigma2_u", "hb[5]"))

Spatial and Spatio-Temporal Structures

Spatial Priors

  1. BYM2 (spatial = "bym2"): The scaled Besag-York-Mollié model (Riebler et al., 2016) decomposes area random effects into a spatial structured component and an unstructured IID component: ud=1τu(1−ϕvd+ϕud*)u_d = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\tau_u}} \left( \sqrt{1 - \phi} \, v_d + \sqrt{\phi} \, u^*_d \right) where ϕ∈[0,1]\phi \in [0, 1] measures the proportion of variance explained by spatial structure and has the penalised complexity (PC) prior P(ϕ<0.5)=0.5P(\phi < 0.5) = 0.5 (Simpson et al., 2017).
  2. Besag ICAR (spatial = "besag"): Intrinsic Conditional Autoregressive spatial model.
  3. SAR area effect (spatial = "sar"): u=(I−ρW)−1εu = (I - \rho W)^{-1}\varepsilon, the random effect of the spatial Fay-Herriot model of eblup_sfh().
  4. Spatial Lag Model (spatial = "slm"): η=(I−ρW)−1(Xβ+ε)\eta = (I - \rho W)^{-1}(X\beta + \varepsilon); the covariates are filtered too, so this is not the model of eblup_sfh().

Temporal Models

When data are observed longitudinally across T≥2T \ge 2 time periods, specify time: - temporal = "rw1": First-order Random Walk (Δtτ∼N(0,σt2)\Delta t_\tau \sim N(0, \sigma_t^2)). - temporal = "rw2": Second-order Random Walk for smooth non-linear temporal trends. - temporal = "ar1": First-order Autoregressive process with autocorrelation |ρt|<1|\rho_t| < 1. - temporal = "iid": Unstructured time random effects.

Space-Time Interaction Structures (st_interaction)

  • "none" (Additive): Separate spatial main effect and temporal trend: ηdt=xdt⊤β+sd+γt\eta_{dt} = x_{dt}^\top \beta + s_d + \gamma_t
  • "domain-specific" (matching tipsae): Domain-specific random walks / AR(1) processes with shared precision: ηdt=xdt⊤β+sd+td,t,td,⋅∼RW1(σt2)\eta_{dt} = x_{dt}^\top \beta + s_d + t_{d, t}, \quad t_{d, \cdot} \sim \text{RW1}(\sigma_t^2)
  • "separable" (matching classical eblup_stfh): Spatial random field evolving dynamically across time with AR(1) temporal correlation.
  • "type1" to "type4": Knorr-Held (2000) interactions δdt\delta_{dt} added to the main effects, ηdt=xdt⊤β+sd+γt+δdt\eta_{dt} = x_{dt}^\top \beta + s_d + \gamma_t + \delta_{dt}:
    • "type1": δdt\delta_{dt} independent (unstructured space ×\times unstructured time);
    • "type2": an independent temporal process for each domain (unstructured space ×\times structured time);
    • "type3": an independent ICAR field for each period (structured space ×\times unstructured time);
    • "type4": an ICAR field evolving with the temporal structure (structured space ×\times structured time).
    "type3" and "type4" need a structured spatial effect ("bym2", "bym", "besag" or "leroux").

Case Study: Spatio-Temporal Beta SAE on Emilia-Romagna Poverty

We demonstrate hb_area() using the Italian poverty dataset emilia from the tipsae package (38 health districts in Emilia-Romagna across 5 years, N=190N = 190). The goal is to estimate the Head Count Ratio (hcr), which represents the proportion of households below the poverty line.

1. Load Data and Construct Spatial Adjacency Matrix 

library(fastsae)
library(tipsae)
library(spdep)

data("emilia")
data("emilia_shp")

# Construct binary spatial adjacency matrix W from district polygons
nb <- poly2nb(emilia_shp)
W <- nb2mat(nb, style = "B", zero.policy = TRUE)
rownames(W) <- colnames(W) <- as.character(emilia_shp$NAME_DISTRICT)

head(emilia[, c("id", "year", "hcr", "vars", "x")])
#>                    id year    hcr         vars       x
#> 1 CASALECCHIO DI RENO 2014 0.0404 9.090478e-05 -0.2624
#> 2   CITTA' DI BOLOGNA 2014 0.0825 6.404001e-05 -0.0008
#> 3               IMOLA 2014 0.1033 3.120275e-04 -0.0522
#> 4         PIANURA EST 2014 0.0633 1.025764e-04 -0.4007
#> 5       PIANURA OVEST 2014 0.0625 1.562500e-04 -0.2277
#> 6      PORRETTA TERME 2014 0.1276 6.643609e-04 -0.4434

2. Fit Spatio-Temporal Beta Model

We model the poverty proportion using a Beta likelihood with a Besag ICAR spatial random effect, a domain-specific RW(1) temporal dynamic, and known sampling variances vars:

fit_beta_st <- hb_area(
  formula = hcr ~ x,
  data = emilia,
  domain = "id",
  time = "year",
  vardir = "vars",
  family = "beta",
  spatial = "besag",
  temporal = "rw1",
  st_interaction = "domain-specific",
  W = W,
  print_result = FALSE
)

summary(fit_beta_st)

Comparison and Validation Against tipsae (Stan MCMC)

In tipsae::fit_sae(..., spatial_error = TRUE, temporal_error = TRUE), the model is estimated by Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) in Stan. fastsae::hb_area() fits a model with the same structure by INLA; the priors of the two packages differ.

Characteristic tipsae::fit_sae (Stan MCMC) fastsae::hb_area (INLA)
Model Beta, Besag ICAR + domain-specific RW(1) spatial = "besag", temporal = "rw1", st_interaction = "domain-specific"
Estimation MCMC (NUTS) Integrated nested Laplace approximation (INLA’s default "compact" mode for Beta)
Execution time 22 min (4 chains x 10,000 iterations, largest R̂\hat R 1.007); 4 chains x 2,000 iterations (120 s) have not converged 1.1 s
Posterior means vs converged tipsae Reference r=0.999r = 0.999, mean absolute difference 0.0017

Measured on 2026-10-16 (tipsae reference refitted on 2026-10-17) on one machine (Apple silicon); times depend on the hardware. The accuracy of hb_area() was also checked against Stan with identical models and priors; see the Engines section of ?hb_area.

Interactive Scalability Explorer (n=30n = 30 to n=1,000n = 1,000)

Use the interactive controls below to compare runtime, memory footprint, and speedup factors between fastsae::hb_area and tipsae::fit_sae across both Standard Beta and Spatial Beta (Besag ICAR) models:

Execution time (median, seconds) — Standard Beta · log scale
Speedup Factor & Efficiency Multiplier (fastsae vs tipsae) — Standard Beta

Agreement with Stan MCMC (Beta model, n=1,000n = 1,000)

To check that the speed of fastsae::hb_area does not come at the cost of its estimates, both packages were fitted with their defaults to the n=1,000n = 1,000 data set of the Beta benchmark (independent area effects, sampling variances from the direct estimates; benchmarks/bench_beta_concordance.R). The two packages do not fit identical models (their priors differ, and fastsae fixes the precision at a first-stage estimate while tipsae makes it a function of the model mean), so the comparison is between what a user obtains from each package:

Metric fastsae::hb_area (INLA) tipsae::fit_sae (Stan)
RMSE against the true area means 0.0678 0.0684
Coverage of the 95% intervals 93.3% 91.1%
Mean width of the 95% intervals 0.252 0.259
Time 4.3 s 184 s

The posterior means of the two packages differed by 0.0096 on average (absolute difference), and the posterior SDs of fastsae were 0.99 times those of tipsae in the median area (90% of the areas between 0.88 and 1.17). The largest R̂\hat{R} of the tipsae fit was 1.008.

Cross-Sectional Count Data: Poisson & Negative Binomial

For count data such as disease incidence or crime events, hb_area() seamlessly supports Poisson and Negative Binomial distributions with population offsets:

# Simulate 42-domain count data with known spatial structure
data("sim_area", package = "fastsae")

# The BYM2 model uses a neighbourhood graph: the 4 nearest centroids of each domain
W_knn <- create_weights(cbind(sim_area$x_coord, sim_area$y_coord), method = "knn", k = 4)

# Fit Poisson Spatial Model with population exposure offset
fit_pois <- hb_area(
  formula = y_poisson ~ x1 + x2,
  data = sim_area,
  exposure = "exposure",
  family = "poisson",
  spatial = "bym2",
  W = W_knn,
  print_result = FALSE
)

summary(fit_pois)
